blocks.content: This closing topic ties together every practice covered across this entire Security module under one core, unifying principle: exactly what is needed, and genuinely nothing more.
1. The Core Principle
Least privilege means granting exactly the access genuinely needed to do a specific, real job, and nothing more, a principle already applied throughout this entire module, now made explicit.
This is not a new, separate idea, it is the single thread running underneath every specific practice covered so far, IAM scoping, backend restriction, secret handling, all of it.
Making this principle explicit, rather than leaving it implicit, makes it considerably easier to apply consistently to new, real situations not explicitly covered elsewhere in this module.
This topic revisits each earlier topic's practices specifically through this one, unifying lens.

blocks.content: 2. Applied to Terraform's Own IAM Role
blocks.text: 2. Applied to Terraform's Own IAM Role

blocks.content: Recall IAM Best Practices, Terraform's own dedicated role should hold exactly the real permissions its actual configuration needs, nothing broader, and nothing left over from an earlier, different need.
This is the most direct, concrete application of least privilege already covered explicitly, worth recognizing now as an instance of this broader, single principle.
A policy that genuinely reflects current, real usage, rather than accumulated historical permissions, is exactly what this principle demands in practice.
Revisiting this specific policy periodically, covered later in this topic, keeps it honestly aligned with this principle over time.

blocks.content: 3. Applied to Backend Access
Recall State Security and Remote Backend Security, restricting access to exactly the identities that genuinely need it is this same principle, applied to the backend specifically.
Block Public Access, a scoped bucket policy, and narrow DynamoDB permissions are all, individually, concrete expressions of this one, same underlying idea.
Seeing these earlier, specific practices as instances of one principle, rather than a disconnected checklist, makes them easier to extend to new, real situations.
This is precisely the value of naming the principle explicitly, here, at the close of this module.

blocks.content: 4. Applied to Real Team Member Access
blocks.text: 4. Applied to Real Team Member Access

blocks.content: Beyond Terraform's own identity, real team members themselves should have access scoped to what each genuinely needs, not broad, shared administrative access by default.
A developer who only ever needs to run plan, reviewing proposed changes, genuinely does not need apply permissions at all in many real, legitimate workflows.
This distinction, plan versus apply access, is a genuinely practical, real way to apply least privilege to human team members specifically.
Real access should map to real, current responsibilities, not accumulate indefinitely as a team and its membership naturally change over time.

5. Separate Roles Per Environment
Recall Environment Isolation from the Workspaces module, separate, scoped IAM roles per environment are this same principle, applied directly as real, practical infrastructure.
Access to production specifically should genuinely be narrower, and more deliberately granted, than access to a lower-stakes dev or staging environment.
This directly addresses the honest limit already covered in Environment Isolation, shared credentials across every workspace by default, with a real, concrete fix.
Implementing this connects two modules directly, workspace structure and IAM access, together forming one coherent, real security posture.

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Concrete Example
A genuinely well-scoped setup might grant a CI pipeline apply access to dev automatically, but require explicit, real human approval before the same pipeline can apply to production.
This reflects exactly the real, honest risk difference between the two environments, dev mistakes are genuinely cheap, production mistakes genuinely are not.
Implementing this specific pattern is covered more fully in the CI/CD Integration module ahead, this topic covers the underlying, real principle behind it.
This concrete example ties together IAM scoping, environment isolation, and real, practical workflow design, all under this one, single principle.

# CI pipeline: auto-apply to dev, require manual approval for production
environment:
  dev: auto-apply
  production: manual-approval-required

blocks.content: 7. The Real Tradeoff: Convenience vs Security
blocks.text: 7. The Real Tradeoff: Convenience vs Security

blocks.content: Genuine, real convenience, broad access, fewer approval steps, sits in real, honest tension with security, exactly the tradeoff this module has touched on from its very first topic.
This tradeoff is genuinely real, not imagined, tighter access does mean real, additional friction for legitimate, everyday work.
The honest, practical answer is not maximum restriction everywhere, it is matching the real level of restriction to the real, actual stakes involved, exactly as covered in Environment Isolation.
Being honest about this tradeoff, rather than pretending it does not exist, is what makes a real security posture sustainable over time.

blocks.content: 8. Reviewing and Tightening Over Time
Access granted once, for a real, specific, and legitimate need, should genuinely be reviewed and tightened over time, not left in place indefinitely.
A real, periodic access review, even just once or twice a year, catches permissions that genuinely outlived their original, legitimate purpose.
This applies to every layer covered throughout this module, Terraform's own IAM role, backend access, and real team member permissions alike.
Building this review into a genuine, recurring team practice, rather than a one-time setup exercise, is what keeps least privilege honestly maintained.

blocks.content: 9. A Real, Common Mistake
Broad access, granted once during an early, urgent setup, and genuinely never revisited afterward, is a real, extremely common mistake across real, production teams.
This often happens with entirely good intentions, moving fast during initial setup, with a real plan to narrow access later that quietly never actually happens.
The honest fix is treating the periodic review covered in the previous section as a genuine, non-negotiable calendar commitment, not an optional aspiration.
Recognizing this as a real, common pattern, rather than a rare failure, is what makes proactively guarding against it genuinely worthwhile.
